questions.text: Acute diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis follows infection by:
questions.explanation: Acute diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (PSGN) follows infection by nephritogenic strains of Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus (e.g., M-types 12, 49) after a latent interval of 1-4 weeks.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1242
questions.text: Acute diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis is due to:
options: Deposition of immune complexes in the glomeruli
questions.explanation: PSGN is a Type III hypersensitivity reaction caused by circulating immune complexes (antigen-antibody) depositing in the subepithelial space as pathognomonic subepithelial humps on electron microscopy.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1246
questions.text: Nephrotic syndrome is NOT characterised by:
questions.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome is clinically defined by massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/24h), severe hypoalbuminemia (<3.0 g/dL), generalized edema, and hyperlipidemia with lipiduria. Gross hematuria and hypertension are characteristic of nephritic, not nephrotic, syndrome.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1248
questions.text: Oedema of the nephritic syndrome is due to:
options: Excessive reabsorption of water and salt by the tubules
Increased hydrostatic pressure of the blood
questions.explanation: Edema in nephritic syndrome is primarily caused by primary renal sodium and water retention due to acute reduction in GFR, leading to circulatory overload and periorbital edema.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1252
questions.text: Epithelial crescents are characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN / crescentic GN) is characterized on light microscopy by circumferential epithelial crescents lining Bowman's space, composed of proliferating parietal epithelial cells and infiltrating monocytes/macrophages.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1253
questions.text: Membrano-proliferative glomerulonephritis is characterised by all  EXCEPT:
options: Infiltration of the glomeruli by polymorphs
Thickening of the glomerular capillary walls
questions.explanation: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN Type I) is characterized by mesangial cell interposition and subendothelial immune deposits causing glomerular basement membrane duplication, creating a classic 'tram-track' or split-basement-membrane appearance on Silver stain.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1254
questions.text: The following change(s) occur in minimal change glomerulonephritis:
options: None of the above (glomeruli appear normal on light microscopy)
questions.explanation: Minimal change disease (lipoid nephrosis) characteristically shows normal glomeruli on light microscopy and negative immunofluorescence, but electron microscopy reveals diffuse, uniform effacement (flattening) of podocyte foot processes.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1256
questions.text: Subepithelial electron dense deposits are characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Membranous nephropathy is defined ultrastructurally by subepithelial electron-dense immune deposits along the glomerular basement membrane, separated by spikes of silver-staining basement membrane matrix ('spike and dome' pattern).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1267
questions.text: Factors predisposing te pyelonephritis include all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Acute pyelonephritis is a suppurative inflammation of the kidney caused predominantly by ascending Gram-negative enteric bacilli (E. coli). Predisposing factors include urinary tract obstruction, vesicoureteral reflux, pregnancy, and diabetes mellitus.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1268
questions.text: Females are more susceptible to urinary tract infection because:
options: The immune system is weaker in females
questions.explanation: Females have a marked anatomical predisposition to ascending urinary tract infections and pyelonephritis due to their significantly shorter urethra and its close anatomical proximity to the fecal flora of the anus.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1269
questions.text: Routes of infection in pyelonephritis:
options: Ascending infection from the urinary bladder
Blood spread from a septic focus
questions.explanation: The predominant and most frequent route of renal infection in acute pyelonephritis is ascending infection from the lower urinary tract up the ureters into the renal pelvis and calyces.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1271
questions.text: Individuals who consume large quantities of analgesics may develop:
questions.explanation: Chronic excessive ingestion of analgesic mixtures (phenacetin, aspirin, acetaminophen) causes chronic interstitial nephritis complicated by ischemic renal papillary necrosis, where necrotic papillae slough into the urine causing ureteric colic and hematuria.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1272
questions.text: Mismatched blood transfusion leads to:
questions.explanation: Mismatched ABO blood transfusion triggers massive intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria, systemic hypotension, and severe ischemic/nephrotoxic Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN), leading to acute oliguric renal failure.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1273
questions.text: Tuberculosis of the kidney is NOT:
questions.explanation: Renal tuberculosis is an active hematogenous metastatic infection secondary to primary pulmonary tuberculosis. It classically begins in the corticomedullary junction, producing caseating fibrocaseous granulomas that cavitate into the calyceal system.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1312
questions.text: Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs may lead to:
questions.explanation: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can induce acute interstitial nephritis characterized by tubular cell injury, interstitial edema, and an inflammatory infiltrate rich in eosinophils and T-lymphocytes.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1259
questions.text: The gross picture of the kidneys in benign hypertension is similar to that of:
questions.explanation: Benign nephrosclerosis in essential hypertension is characterized grossly by symmetrical, moderately reduced kidneys with a fine, granular, pebbled cortical surface resembling leather ('grain leather' appearance) due to patchy cortical atrophy.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1260
questions.text: Flea-bitten kidney is a gross feature of:
questions.explanation: Malignant hypertension is characterized by widespread hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis ('onion-skinning') and necrotizing arteriolitis with fibrinoid necrosis, producing petechial cortical hemorrhages termed a 'flea-bitten' kidney.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1262
questions.text: Diabetic nephropathy does NOT predisposes to:
questions.explanation: Diabetic nephropathy is characterized by diffuse glomerulosclerosis and pathognomonic nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules), accompanied by severe arteriolar hyalinosis affecting BOTH afferent and efferent arterioles.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1263
questions.text: The most common type of giomerulonephritis seen in lupus nephritis is:
questions.explanation: In systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), Class IV Diffuse Proliferative Lupus Nephritis is the most common, most severe, and most aggressive histological subtype, requiring intensive immunosuppressive therapy.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1264
questions.text: Wire loop appearance in the glomeruli is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Wire loop lesions in lupus nephritis represent extensive, confluent subendothelial immune complex deposits that markedly thicken the glomerular capillary walls, resembling rigid bent wires on light microscopy.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1265
questions.text: Good-Pasteur’s syndrome is characterised by all EXCEPT:
options: Most frequent in young adults ~~ E. Pulmonary haemorrhages
questions.explanation: Goodpasture syndrome is caused by circulating autoantibodies directed against the non-collagenous domain (NC1) of alpha-3 chain of collagen type IV in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, producing rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary alveolar hemorrhage.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1274
questions.text: The following thrombus does NOT send emboli to the renal arteries:
questions.explanation: Renal arterial infarction is typically caused by thromboembolism originating from mural thrombi in the left heart (atrial fibrillation, left ventricular MI) or severe atherosclerotic aortic plaques, producing wedge-shaped pale, coagulative cortical infarcts.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1258
questions.text: Gross features of the kidneys in chronic glomerulonephritis include all  EXCEPT:
options: Contraction of the kidneys is asymmetrical
Cut surface shows thick-walled blood vessels
questions.explanation: End-stage chronic glomerulonephritis produces markedly contracted, symmetrically shrunken kidneys with a diffusely granular thinned cortex, obliterated corticomedullary junction, and global hyalinization/sclerosis of glomeruli.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1286
questions.text: The following is a cause of acute renal failure:
questions.explanation: Acute renal failure (acute kidney injury) can result from prerenal hypoperfusion (shock, dehydration), intrinsic acute tubular necrosis (ischemic or toxic), or postrenal acute bilateral urinary tract obstruction.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1238
questions.text: Horse-shoe kidney is a:
questions.explanation: Horseshoe kidney is the most common congenital fusion anomaly, where the lower poles of the kidneys are fused across the midline anterior to the abdominal aorta and IVC, trapped inferiorly by the origin of the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1239
questions.text: Adult polycystic kidney is characterised by all EXCEPT:
options: Inherited as an autosomal dominant trait
Shows multiple cysts communicating with the pelvis
questions.explanation: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD, PKD1/PKD2 genes) is characterized by bilaterally massively enlarged kidneys filled with multiple non-communicating fluid-filled cysts lined by flattened epithelium, inexorably causing ESRD in adulthood.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1316
questions.text: A male patient with a long history of pulmonary tuberculosis, is now  suffering from chronic renal failure. The most possible cause is:
questions.explanation: In long-standing chronic suppurative or tuberculous disease, renal secondary (AA) amyloidosis develops, manifesting with pale, waxy, enlarged kidneys with positive Congo Red staining showing apple-green birefringence under polarized light.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1317
questions.text: A 40 years old woman presented with chronic renal failure.  Pyelography showed dilation of the pelvicalyceal system. Renal biopsy  revealed tubular atrophy, periglomerular fibrosis and interstitial  inflammatory cells. The most possible diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Chronic pyelonephritis produces characteristically asymmetric, irregularly scarred kidneys with deep, broad, U-shaped corticomedullary depressions overlying blunted, dilated, deformed calyces (calyceal clubbing).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1319
questions.text: A child suffering from post streptococcal glomerulonephritis may die  due to:
questions.explanation: The most common and immediate cause of death in children with acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is acute heart failure and pulmonary edema secondary to severe hypervolemic fluid overload, or hypertensive encephalopathy.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1288
questions.text: Gross features of renal cell carcinoma include all EXCEPT:
options: It 1s commonly centred in the cortex
It 1s surrounded by a true capsule
questions.explanation: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) typically originates in the renal cortex as a golden-yellow, circumscribed mass with prominent areas of hemorrhage, necrosis, and cystic degeneration, characteristically invading the renal vein.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1294
questions.text: VHL gene mutation may occur in:
questions.explanation: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (the commonest RCC subtype, 70-80%) is strongly associated with loss or inactivation of the VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3p, leading to constitutive HIF-1alpha activation and VEGF overexpression.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1295
questions.text: MET proto-oncogene is mutated in:
questions.explanation: Papillary renal cell carcinoma (10-15% of RCCs) is characterized by trisomy 7 and 17 and activating mutations or duplications of the MET proto-oncogene encoding the hepatocyte growth factor receptor.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1287
questions.text: The following tumor is Common in children:
questions.explanation: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) is the most common primary malignant renal tumor of childhood (peak age 2-5 years), arising from primitive metanephric blastema and associated with WT1 gene mutations on chromosome 11p13.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1293
questions.text: The blastomatous tissue consists of:
questions.explanation: Classic Wilms tumor exhibits a characteristic triphasic histology consisting of: primitive blastematous sheets of small round blue cells, epithelial tubular/glomeruloid structures, and mesenchymal stroma (spindle cells, skeletal muscle, cartilage).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1321
questions.text: An adult female patient presented with generalized edema. Labarotory  investigations revealed hypoalbuminemia and proteinuria. Renal  biopsy showed diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement  membrane with granular deposits of IgG by immunofluorescence. The  most possible diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Adult renal oncocytoma is a benign epithelial neoplasm derived from intercalated cells of collecting ducts, characterized grossly by a mahogany-brown color with a prominent central stellate scar, and histologically by sheets of uniform eosinophilic cells packed with mitochondria.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1322
questions.text: A female patient S0 year old presented with oligunia and hematuria.  Kidney function tests revaled increased blood urea. Renal biopsy  showed large subcapsular epithelial crescents in some glomemli. The  renal tubules contained red cell casts. The most possible diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Renal angiomyolipoma is a benign mesenchymal hamartoma composed of mature adipose tissue, smooth muscle, and thick-walled dysplastic blood vessels, frequently associated with tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2 mutations).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1281
questions.text: The following type of renal stones usually has a stag horn appearance:
questions.explanation: Staghorn calculi are large branched stones that fill the renal pelvis and calyces, composed of magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite/triple phosphate) caused by urease-producing bacterial infections (Proteus mirabilis).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1282
questions.text: The following type of renal stones is radio-translucent:
questions.explanation: Uric acid calculi develop in acidic urine (pH < 5.5) and are uniquely radiolucent on conventional plain abdominal radiographs (KUB), requiring non-contrast CT for radiographic visualization.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1283
questions.text: The following type of renal stones is multiple and spiky:
questions.explanation: Calcium oxalate calculi are the most common type of urinary stones (70-80%); they are hard, radio-opaque, and frequently have a dark brown, spiky, mulberriform or jackstone appearance that scratches the urothelium causing hematuria.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1297
questions.text: Schistosomiasis of the bladder predisposes to:
questions.explanation: Urinary schistosomiasis (Schistosoma haematobium) causes chronic urothelial ulceration, inflammation, and squamous metaplasia, predisposing heavily to invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) of the urinary bladder.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1299
questions.text: The gross feature of malakoplakia of the bladder mucosa is:
questions.explanation: Malakoplakia of the urinary bladder is an inflammatory pseudotumor associated with chronic E. coli cystitis, characterized histologically by sheets of foamy histiocytes (von Hansemann cells) containing laminated, basophilic, calcified concentric inclusions called Michaelis-Gutmann bodies.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1303
questions.text: Dye workers are at risk of developing:
questions.explanation: Occupational exposure to aromatic amines (aniline dyes, 2-naphthylamine, benzidine) in textile, chemical, and rubber industries is a major established risk factor for urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma of the urinary bladder.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1307
questions.text: The most improtant prognostic factor in bladder carcinoma is:
questions.explanation: In staging bladder urothelial carcinoma, the single most critical prognostic factor determining survival and management (transurethral resection vs. radical cystectomy) is the depth of tumor invasion into the muscularis propria (detrusor muscle, stage T2).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1354
questions.text: Cryptorchidism means:
questions.explanation: Cryptorchidism refers to the failure of one or both testes to descend completely into the scrotum, arresting in the inguinal canal or abdomen; it causes tubular atrophy, hyalinization, azoospermia, and carries a 3- to 5-fold increased risk of testicular germ cell cancer.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1363
questions.text: Seminoma is characterised by all EXCEPT:
options: It may be of the anaplastic or spermatocytic type
The stroma often shows epithelioid granulomas
questions.explanation: Testicular seminoma is the most common germ cell tumor (peak age 30-40), characterized by sheets of uniform polyhedral cells with clear glycogen-rich cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, prominent nucleoli, and delicate fibrovascular septa infiltrated by T-lymphocytes.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1365
questions.text: The following tumor secretes alpha fetoprotein:
questions.explanation: Testicular yolk sac tumor (endodermal sinus tumor) is the most common testicular neoplasm in infants and boys under 3 years of age, characterized by elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and pathognomonic Schiller-Duval bodies mimicking primitive glomeruli.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1367
questions.text: The following tumor secretes placental alkaline phosphatase:
questions.explanation: Testicular choriocarcinoma is a highly aggressive malignant germ cell tumor composed of syncytiotrophoblasts and cytotrophoblasts, characteristically producing massive elevations in serum beta-hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) and early hematogenous metastases.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1374
questions.text: The commonest type of malignancy in malignant teratoma is:
questions.explanation: Post-pubertal testicular teratoma is considered malignant regardless of its histological maturity (mature vs. immature components), capable of late aggressive metastasis, unlike benign childhood teratomas.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1356
questions.text: Syphilitic orchitis occurs in:
questions.explanation: Syphilitic orchitis classically presents in tertiary syphilis as a painless gumma or chronic interstitial fibrosis with obliterative endarteritis, characteristically sparing the epididymis (unlike tuberculosis which primarily affects the epididymis).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1357
questions.text: Tuberculous epididymitis results from:
questions.explanation: Tuberculous epididymitis is almost always secondary to retrograde canalicular or hematogenous spread from the urinary tract (kidney/prostate), causing caseating granulomas that begin in the globus minor of the epididymis before invading the testis.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1380
questions.text: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is explained by the increase in the  following
questions.explanation: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) arises exclusively in the periurethral and transition zones of the prostate under the trophic hormonal influence of dihydrotestosterone (DHT) synthesized by stromal 5alpha-reductase.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1382
questions.text: Perineural invasion is most commonly seen in:
questions.explanation: Perineural space invasion is a characteristic histological hallmark of prostatic adenocarcinoma, where malignant glands wrap around or infiltrate intramural autonomic nerve twigs within the prostatic capsule and periprostatic fat.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1384
questions.text: The following marker is used for diagnosis of prostatic carcinoma:
questions.explanation: Serum Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) is an organ-specific (not cancer-specific) serine protease secreted by prostatic epithelial cells; serum levels >4 ng/mL warrant further evaluation, while PSA velocity and free-to-total PSA ratio assist in differentiating BPH from carcinoma.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1389
questions.text: Bone metastases from prostatic carcinoma are osteoblastic because the  tumor secretes:
questions.explanation: Skeletal metastases from prostatic adenocarcinoma characteristically stimulate osteoblast proliferation and new woven bone deposition, producing dense, radio-opaque osteoblastic (osteosclerotic) bone lesions on plain radiographs and bone scans.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1397
questions.text: Gleason's grading system for prostatic carcinoma is important for:
questions.explanation: The Gleason grading system for prostatic adenocarcinoma is based entirely on histological architectural growth patterns (patterns 1 through 5) rather than cytological atypia, combining the primary and secondary patterns to yield a prognostic Gleason score.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1399
questions.text: Complications of prostatic hyperplasia include all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Major clinical complications of benign prostatic hyperplasia include bladder outlet obstruction, detrusor hypertrophy and trabeculation, bladder diverticula, urinary stasis with recurrent UTIs, bilateral hydronephrosis, and postrenal azotemia.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1404
questions.text: Amale patient 60 year old complained of dysuria and hematuria.  Rectal examination showed enlargement of the prostate. Serum  prostatic specific antigen was normal. The most possible diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Prostatic adenocarcinoma arises in >70% of cases in the peripheral (posterior) zone of the prostate, which explains why it is palpable on digital rectal examination (DRE) as a hard, irregular nodule before producing early obstructive symptoms.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1426
questions.text: Condyloma accuminatum is not characterised by:
options: It is induced by Epstein Barr virus
It consists of proliferating squamous epithelium
questions.explanation: Condyloma acuminatum of the external genitalia is a benign verrucous squamous papilloma caused by low-risk Human Papillomavirus types 6 and 11, histologically characterized by branching acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, and superficial koilocytosis.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1427
questions.text: Condyloma lata are caused by:
questions.explanation: Condyloma lata are moist, flat, broad, highly infectious mucosal plaques of the vulva, perineum, or scrotum, representing a classical mucocutaneous manifestation of secondary syphilis teeming with Treponema pallidum spirochetes.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1429
questions.text: Paget’s disease is a:
questions.explanation: Extramammary Paget disease of the vulva or scrotum manifests as an erythematous, crusted, pruritic plaque, histologically characterized by intraepithelial infiltration of large malignant glandular cells with pale mucinous cytoplasm (mucin-positive, PAS-positive).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1433
questions.text: The following lesion appears as whitish plaques of the vulva:
questions.explanation: Lichen sclerosus of the vulva (kraurosis vulvae) manifests clinically as smooth white porcelain-like atrophic plaques ('leukoplakia'), histologically showing epidermal thinning, hydropic basal degeneration, and a broad band of dense dermal collagen homogenization/hyalinization.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1434
questions.text: The following lesion does NOT predispose to invasive carcinoma:
questions.explanation: Lichen simplex chronicus of the vulva results from chronic scratching or rubbing; it is characterized histologically by marked epidermal hyperkeratosis and acanthosis with regular rete ridge elongation, carrying no intrinsic premalignant potential.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1435
questions.text: Sarcoma botryoides is a type of:
questions.explanation: Sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma) is the most common malignant vaginal/urinary tract sarcoma in infants and young girls under 5 years, presenting grossly as soft, gelatinous polypoid masses resembling a 'bunch of grapes' protruding from the introitus.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1436
questions.text: The commonest malignant vaginal tumor in childhood is:
questions.explanation: Invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the penis is strongly associated with lack of neonatal circumcision (poor hygiene/smegma accumulation) and high-risk HPV types 16 and 18, commonly arising on the glans penis or inner surface of the prepuce.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1437
questions.text: The following is NOT a feature of the endocervical polyp:
questions.explanation: Endocervical polyps are benign inflammatory inflammatory outgrowths of endocervical mucosa, composed of loose fibromyxomatous vascular stroma lined by mucus-secreting columnar epithelium, frequently presenting with postcoital spotting.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1439
questions.text: The nuclear features of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia include all  EXCEDPT :
options: Decreased nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio   E. Increased mitotic activity
questions.explanation: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is characterized cytologically by nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, coarse chromatin clumping, irregular nuclear contours, pleomorphism, and abnormal mitotic figures starting in the basal layers.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1440
questions.text: Grading of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) depends on:  A Thickness of the epithelium showing loss of maturation
questions.explanation: Histological grading of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia depends on the vertical extent of squamous epithelial dysplasia: CIN 1 involves the lower 1/3; CIN 2 involves the lower 2/3; and CIN 3 involves more than 2/3 to full-thickness dysplasia (carcinoma in situ).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1443
questions.text: The best method used as a screening test for cervical cancer is:
questions.explanation: The Papanicolaou (Pap) cervical cytology smear combined with high-risk HPV DNA co-testing is the worldwide standard screening method, sampling cells from the cervical transformation zone (squamocolumnar junction) to detect pre-invasive dysplastic lesions.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1444
questions.text: Carcinoma in situ means:  A Dysplastic changes involving lower 1/3 of epithelium
options: Dysplastic changes involving lower 2/3 of epithelium
Dysplastic changes involving more than 2/3 of epithelium
Dysplastic changes involving whole thickness of epithelium
Dysplastic changes involving whole thickness of epithelium with  koilocytic changes
questions.explanation: Carcinoma in situ (CIN 3) of the uterine cervix is defined histologically as full-thickness squamous atypia and loss of maturation spanning the entire epithelial height, but strictly contained above an intact basement membrane without stromal microinvasion.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1445
questions.text: HPV induces cervical carcinoma through:  A Induction of koilocytosis
options: Expression of E6 and E7 proteins
questions.explanation: High-risk HPV types 16 and 18 induce cervical oncogenesis primarily through integration of viral DNA into host genome, leading to overexpression of oncoproteins E6 (which promotes ubiquitin-dependent degradation of p53) and E7 (which binds and inactivates retinoblastoma pRb).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1511
questions.text: The most important risk factor for cervical cancer is:
questions.explanation: Persistent high-risk Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection (especially genotypes 16, 18, 31, 33, 45) is the single most critical and mandatory epidemiological risk factor for the development of invasive cervical carcinoma.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1450
questions.text: The following endometrial changes indicate ovulation:
questions.explanation: Under light microscopy, the histological hallmark confirming normal ovulation and the onset of the endometrial secretory phase is the appearance of uniform subnuclear glycogen vacuoles within columnar glandular epithelial cells on day 16-17.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1456
questions.text: The most important complication of endometrial hyperplasia is:
questions.explanation: Endometrial hyperplasia without atypia carries a <1-3% risk of progression to adenocarcinoma, whereas atypical endometrial hyperplasia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia, EIN) carries an alarming 20-30% risk of concurrent or future invasive carcinoma.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1457
questions.text: The most common tumor in females is:
questions.explanation: Uterine leiomyoma (fibroid) is the most common benign mesenchymal tumor in women of reproductive age, arising from myometrial smooth muscle cells and characterized by whorled bundles of uniform spindle cells surrounded by a distinct pseudocapsule.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1461
questions.text: Swiss cheese appearance is a feature of:
questions.explanation: Simple non-atypical endometrial hyperplasia characteristically exhibits dilated, cystic, irregular glands lined by non-stratified columnar cells with no cellular atypia, producing a classic 'Swiss-cheese' architectural appearance.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1463
questions.text: Endometriosis is defined as:
options: Presence of endometrial glands in abnormal sites
Presence of endometrial stroma in abnormal sites
Presence of endometrial glands and stroma in abnormal sites
Presence of endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterine wall
questions.explanation: Endometriosis is defined pathologically as the presence of functional endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterine cavity, most frequently affecting the ovaries (forming 'chocolate cysts' / endometriomas), pelvic peritoneum, and pouch of Douglas.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1467
questions.text: The most important risk factor for endometrial carcinoma is:
questions.explanation: Type I endometrioid adenocarcinoma of the endometrium (accounting for 80% of cases) is strongly driven by prolonged, unopposed hyperestrogenism (obesity, nulliparity, late menopause, estrogen replacement therapy, PCOS) and PTEN mutations.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1469
questions.text: The most aggressive type of endometrial carcinoma is:
questions.explanation: Type II serous carcinoma of the endometrium is an aggressive, estrogen-independent tumor occurring in elderly women with atrophic endometria, strongly associated with TP53 mutations, extensive pelvic dissemination, and poor clinical prognosis.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1472
questions.text: Hydatidiform mole occurs in:
questions.explanation: Complete hydatidiform mole results from androgenesis: fertilization of an enucleate (empty) ovum by a single sperm that duplicates (46,XX, 90%) or by two sperm (46,XY), producing purely paternal genetic material with no maternal chromosomes.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1473
questions.text: Complete vesicular mole is NOT characterised by:
options: High levels of serum chorionic gonadotropin
Small vesicles in the evacuated mole
questions.explanation: Complete hydatidiform mole is characterized by diffuse, circumferential trophoblastic hyperplasia, generalized hydropic swelling of all chorionic villi with central cistern formation, markly elevated serum beta-hCG (>100,000 mIU/mL), and COMPLETE ABSENCE of fetal or embryonic tissues.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1474
questions.text: Partial vesicular mole is NOT characterised by:
options: Low levels of serum chorionic gonadotropin
Small vesicles in the evacuated mole
questions.explanation: Partial hydatidiform mole results from diandric triploidy: fertilization of a normal haploid ovum (23,X) by two sperm (or a diploid sperm), resulting in a 69,XXX, 69,XXY, or 69,XYY karyotype, and characteristically DOES contain fetal or embryonic parts.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1478
questions.text: Fertilization of normal egg by two spermatozoa results in:
questions.explanation: Fertilization of a normal haploid ovum by two normal spermatozoa produces a triploid (69 chromosomes) conceptus, which pathologically manifests as a partial vesicular mole with scalloped, focal villous edema and identifiable fetal RBCs.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1479
questions.text: The following does NOT show fetal parts:
questions.explanation: In contrast to partial hydatidiform mole or blighted ovum, a complete hydatidiform mole contains NO fetal parts, no umbilical cord, no amniotic membrane, and no nucleated fetal red blood cells within villous capillaries.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1481
questions.text: The following carcinoma is curable:
questions.explanation: Gestational choriocarcinoma is a highly malignant, invasive epithelial neoplasm composed of anaplastic syncytiotrophoblasts and cytotrophoblasts with extensive hemorrhage and necrosis and NO chorionic villi; it responds spectacularly to chemotherapy (Methotrexate) with >90% cure rates.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1507
questions.text: A 35 year pregnant female suffered from vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound  showed no features. Microscopic exmination of the tissue obtained by  endometrial currettage showed malignant -cytotrophoblast and  syncytiotrophoblast. The most possible diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Pelvic ultrasonography of a complete hydatidiform mole characteristically displays an enlarged uterine cavity filled with a diffuse, heterogeneous, echogenic mass containing innumerable tiny cystic spaces, termed the 'snowstorm' or 'bunch of grapes' appearance.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1484
questions.text: The commonest site of ectopic pregnancy is:
questions.explanation: Ectopic pregnancy occurs when a fertilized blastocyst implants outside the endometrial cavity, with >95% of cases implanting in the fallopian tube (most commonly in the ampulla), predisposed by chronic salpingitis and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1486
questions.text: Stein-Leventhal syndrome consists of all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS / Stein-Leventhal syndrome) is clinically characterized by hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne), chronic anovulation (oligomenorrhea), and bilaterally enlarged ovaries with multiple subcapsular follicular cysts and cortical stromal fibrosis.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1490
questions.text: Ovarian serous cystadenoma is characterised by all EXCEPT:
options: Epithelial lining resembles that of the endometrium
questions.explanation: Serous cystadenoma of the ovary is the most common benign ovarian epithelial neoplasm, typically unilocular, containing clear watery straw-colored serous fluid and lined by a single layer of ciliated columnar epithelial cells resembling tubal mucosa.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1491
questions.text: Ovarian mucinous cystadenoma is characterised by all EXCEPT:
options: Epithelial lining resembles that of the fallopian tube
questions.explanation: Mucinous cystadenoma of the ovary is a multilocular, bulky tumor filled with thick, gelatinous, glycoprotein-rich mucin, lined by non-ciliated columnar epithelial cells with apical mucin vacuoles resembling endocervical or intestinal epithelium.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1493
questions.text: Psammoma bodies may occur in the following ovarian tumor:
questions.explanation: Psammoma bodies are concentric, laminated, basophilic calcospherites that are characteristically found in ovarian serous cystadenocarcinoma (as well as papillary thyroid carcinoma and meningioma).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1496
questions.text: The following ovarian tumor secretes oestrogen:
questions.explanation: Granulosa cell tumors of the ovary are sex cord-stromal neoplasms that characteristically secrete estrogens, causing endometrial hyperplasia, irregular uterine bleeding, or precocious puberty; histologically they feature Call-Exner bodies (microfollicles containing eosinophilic fluid).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1500
questions.text: Dermoid cyst of the ovary is a:
questions.explanation: Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst) is a benign germ cell tumor composed of well-differentiated tissues derived from all three germ cell layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm), characteristically containing hair, sebaceous material, teeth, and keratinaceous debris.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1503
questions.text: Regarding Krukenberg tumors, the following is NOT true:
options: The primary site 1s the gastrointestinal tract
Primary tumor spreads to the ovary by blood
questions.explanation: Krukenberg tumor is a metastatic adenocarcinoma to the ovaries, characteristically bilateral, originating predominantly from gastric signet-ring cell adenocarcinoma (or colon/breast) and histologically displaying mucin-filled signet-ring cells infiltrating ovarian stroma.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1559
questions.text: The ductal-lobular system of the breast is normally lined by:
options: Inner epithelial and outer myoepithelial cells
Outer epithelial and inner myoepithelial cells
questions.explanation: The normal terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU) of the human breast is composed of a two-cell epithelial bilayer consisting of: an inner secretory luminal epithelial cell layer and an outer contractile myoepithelial cell layer.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1560

questions.text: A 60-year-old woman is admitted for cardiogenic shock following acute myocardial infarction. questions.modelAnswer:
Raloxifene is a Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM):
1. Estrogen Agonist on Bone: Preserves bone mineral density and prevents osteoporotic fractures by inhibiting osteoclastic resorption; also acts as an agonist on serum lipid profiles (lowers LDL cholesterol).
2. Estrogen Antagonist on Breast: Competitively blocks estrogen receptors in mammary tissue, reducing the risk of estrogen receptor-positive invasive breast cancer.
3. Estrogen Antagonist on Endometrium/Uterus: Unlike tamoxifen, raloxifene does not stimulate endometrial proliferation and is not associated with an increased risk of endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma.

questions.modelAnswer:
A 'drug holiday' refers to the intentional temporary discontinuation of the potassium-wasting diuretic (e.g., omitting the diuretic for 1–2 days per week or on weekends).
Clinical Rationale:
1. Allows renal tubular recovery and re-accumulation of total body potassium, reducing the risk of severe hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and cardiac arrhythmias (especially in patients taking digitalis/digoxin).
2. Minimizes chronic activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS).
3. Reduces electrolyte-induced refractoriness and diuretic resistance.

questions.text: If a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction occurs following the initiation of penicillin therapy for syphilis, benzathine penicillin treatment should be discontinued immediately.
questions.explanation:
**Correct Answer: False**

**Pharmacological & Clinical Rationale:**
The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is an acute, self-limiting febrile systemic reaction (fever, chills, headache, tachycardia, myalgias, and transient exacerbation of skin lesions) occurring within 2–24 hours after starting antimicrobial therapy for spirochetal infections (especially syphilis). It is caused by the massive release of endotoxin-like inflammatory pyrogens and cytokines from rapidly dying *Treponema pallidum*. It is NOT an IgE-mediated allergic reaction to penicillin, and penicillin therapy MUST NOT be discontinued. Management is supportive, consisting of reassurance, bed rest, and antipyretics (e.g. acetaminophen/paracetamol).

**Curriculum Reference:**
Ain Shams University Urogenital Module Textbook, Pharmacology of Sexually Transmitted Infections, pp. 110–114.

questions.text: Mention the mechanisms of action, clinical therapeutic uses, and major adverse effects of androgen therapy (testosterone):
questions.explanation: Authoritative Ain Shams pharmacology of androgens.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Mechanism of Action: Testosterone diffuses into target cells and binds to intracellular androgen receptors (either directly or after conversion by 5α-reductase to 5α-dihydrotestosterone, DHT). The activated receptor complex acts as a transcription factor, modulating expression of androgen-responsive genes.
2. Therapeutic Uses:
   - Replacement therapy for primary or secondary male hypogonadism.
   - Treatment of delayed puberty in boys.
   - Severe catabolic muscle-wasting states and certain refractory anemias.
   - Palliative treatment of advanced metastatic breast cancer in postmenopausal women.
3. Major Adverse Effects:
   - In females: Virilization, hirsutism, deepening of voice, and menstrual irregularities.
   - In males: Priapism, oligospermia, testicular atrophy (via gonadotropin suppression), and gynecomastia.
   - Systemic: Fluid retention, polycythemia, premature epiphyseal closure in children, and cholestatic jaundice/hepatotoxicity (with oral 17α-alkylated androgens).

questions.text: Which of the following pharmacological agents is strictly CONTRAINDICATED in the acute management of severe symptomatic hyponatremia?
questions.explanation: Desmopressin (dDAVP) is a synthetic V2 receptor agonist that promotes renal free water retention, which would dangerously worsen hyponatremia and exacerbate cerebral edema. In contrast, 3% hypertonic saline, loop diuretics, and vaptans (in non-acute settings) promote water clearance or sodium repletion.

questions.text: To prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis), the maximum recommended rate of correction for chronic hyponatremia is:
options: 18 to 24 mEq/L within the first 24 hours
12 to 18 mEq/L in the first 12 hours
Less than 8 to 10 mEq/L within the first 24 hours (and <18 mEq/L in 48 hours)
More than 20 mEq/L within the first 48 hours
questions.explanation: Rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia causes sudden dehydration of brain oligodendrocytes, triggering osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis). The rate of correction must strictly not exceed 8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours and <18 mEq/L in 48 hours.

questions.text: In correcting acute severe hypernatremia, what is the maximum recommended daily reduction in serum sodium to avoid cerebral edema?
questions.explanation: In hypernatremia, brain cells accumulate idiogenic osmoles to defend cell volume. Overly rapid reduction of serum sodium creates an osmotic gradient drawing water into brain cells, causing cerebral edema and seizures. The safe limit is a maximum reduction of 10 mEq/L daily.

questions.text: Which of the following substances induces hypokalemia and hypertension by inhibiting 11beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (11beta-HSD2)?
questions.explanation: Glycyrrhizin in natural liquorice inhibits renal 11beta-HSD2, preventing the normal enzymatic conversion of cortisol to inactive cortisone. Uninactivated cortisol binds renal mineralocorticoid receptors with high affinity, stimulating excessive sodium reabsorption and potassium wasting (apparent mineralocorticoid excess).

questions.text: In a patient with severe hyperkalemia displaying peaked T waves and widened QRS complexes, which intravenous drug is administered immediately to antagonize cardiac membrane excitability without altering serum potassium levels?
questions.explanation: Intravenous Calcium gluconate membrane-stabilizes cardiac myocytes by restoring normal resting membrane potential thresholds and preventing fatal ventricular arrhythmias. It acts within minutes but does not alter serum potassium concentration.

questions.text: Which pharmacological regimen rapidly drives extracellular potassium into intracellular compartments within 15 to 30 minutes in acute hyperkalemia?
options: Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate with sorbitol
Intravenous regular insulin combined with 50% dextrose
questions.explanation: Insulin stimulates the Na+/K+-ATPase pump on skeletal muscle and hepatocytes, driving potassium into cells within 15-30 minutes. Dextrose is co-administered to prevent hypoglycemia.

questions.text: Which diuretic acts on the thick ascending limb of Henle by reversibly inhibiting the apical Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2)?
questions.explanation: Loop diuretics (Furosemide, Bumetanide, Torsemide) bind the chloride site of the NKCC2 cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of Henle, producing profound diuresis and natriuresis and dissipating the corticomedullary osmotic gradient.

questions.text: Which characteristic metabolic disturbance is commonly produced by high-dose chronic loop diuretic therapy?
questions.explanation: Loop diuretics increase distal delivery of sodium and water, stimulating aldosterone-mediated H+ and K+ excretion in the collecting duct, while volume contraction stimulates bicarbonate reabsorption, producing hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.

questions.text: Which oral vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist is specifically approved for the management of euvolemic (SIADH) and hypervolemic (heart failure, cirrhosis) hyponatremia?
questions.explanation: Tolvaptan is an oral selective vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist that promotes aquaresis (electrolyte-free water excretion) without causing sodium loss, effectively raising serum sodium in SIADH and hypervolemic states.

questions.text: Which carbonic anhydrase inhibitor acts in the renal proximal convoluted tubule to induce sodium bicarbonate diuresis and alkalinize the urine?
questions.explanation: Acetazolamide inhibits membrane-bound and cytosolic carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, blocking bicarbonate reabsorption and producing self-limiting urinary alkalinization and metabolic acidosis.

questions.text: An ideal antibiotic for treating acute uncomplicated lower cystitis should possess all the following pharmacokinetics EXCEPT:
options: Rapid and high concentration in renal parenchymal tissue rather than urine
High concentration of active drug eliminated in the urine
Minimal disturbance of vaginal and intestinal normal flora
Convenient dosing schedule with low adverse effect profile
questions.explanation: For lower cystitis, high renal tissue concentration is NOT necessary; what is crucial is high urinary concentration of active, unmetabolized drug (e.g., Nitrofurantoin, Fosfomycin). High renal parenchymal and bloodstream concentrations are needed for upper UTIs (acute pyelonephritis).

questions.text: Regarding the duration of antimicrobial therapy in urinary tract infections, which of the following statements is INCORRECT?
options: Single-dose therapy (e.g., Fosfomycin 3g) is suitable for uncomplicated lower cystitis in non-pregnant women
Single-day antibiotic therapy is adequate and recommended for UTI in males
7-day therapy is recommended for mild complicated UTIs and during pregnancy
14-day therapy is recommended for acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis
questions.explanation: UTIs in males are by definition considered complicated (due to anatomical factors, risk of prostatitis or urethral obstruction) and must NEVER be treated with single-day therapy; they require at least 7 to 14 days of antimicrobials.

questions.text: In the management of outpatient acute pyelonephritis in an otherwise healthy non-pregnant woman, which class of antibiotics is the first-line oral empirical choice when local resistance is <10%?
questions.explanation: Oral fluoroquinolones (Ciprofloxacin 500mg BID for 7 days or Levofloxacin 750mg daily for 5 days) achieve excellent tissue and serum concentrations in the renal parenchyma and are first-line for acute pyelonephritis. Nitrofurantoin and Fosfomycin do not achieve therapeutic renal tissue levels and must not be used for pyelonephritis.

questions.text: Which antibiotic is considered safe for treating lower urinary tract infections throughout all trimesters of pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Beta-lactams (Cephalexin, Cefuroxime, Amoxicillin-clavulanate) are Category B and completely safe throughout all trimesters of pregnancy. Fluoroquinolones (cartilage toxicity), Tetracyclines (bone/tooth defects), and Sulfonamides in the 3rd trimester (kernicterus) are contraindicated.

questions.text: Why must sulfonamides (such as sulfamethoxazole) be strictly avoided during the third trimester of pregnancy?
options: They cause congenital limb reduction defects
They displace bilirubin from albumin, increasing the risk of neonatal kernicterus
They cause maternal acute liver failure
They induce premature closure of the ductus arteriosus
questions.explanation: Sulfonamides compete with bilirubin for binding sites on fetal/neonatal plasma albumin, raising free unconjugated bilirubin which crosses the immature blood-brain barrier and causes fatal kernicterus.

questions.text: Which first-line lower UTI antimicrobial is concentrated in urine via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, but is CONTRAINDICATED in patients with GFR < 30 mL/min due to inadequate urinary levels and risk of peripheral neuropathy?
questions.explanation: Nitrofurantoin requires adequate GFR to achieve bactericidal concentrations in the urine. When GFR is <30 mL/min, urinary levels are subtherapeutic while systemic accumulation causes severe toxicity, including peripheral neuropathy and pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.text: Fosfomycin tromethamine is unique as an oral first-line agent for acute uncomplicated cystitis because:
options: It is given as a single 3-gram oral sachet that maintains therapeutic urinary concentrations for 48 hours
It requires a 14-day continuous oral course
It is an aminoglycoside that must be monitored with peak and trough levels
It is only effective against Gram-positive anaerobes
questions.explanation: Fosfomycin tromethamine inhibits bacterial MurA (early peptidoglycan synthesis) and is administered as a single 3g oral dose dissolved in water, providing sustained bactericidal urinary concentrations for up to 2-3 days.

questions.text: Why is screening and treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) mandatory in pregnant women, but not in non-pregnant premenopausal women?
options: ASB in pregnancy carries a 20-30 fold increased risk of progressing to acute pyelonephritis, preterm labor, and low birth weight
It always leads to fetal congenital heart disease
Pregnancy induces complete resistance to all cephalosporins
ASB in pregnancy indicates systemic bacteremia
questions.explanation: Pregnancy-induced ureteral dilation, decreased bladder tone, and physiological hydronephrosis allow ascending infection; untreated ASB progresses to pyelonephritis in up to 30% of pregnant women, directly increasing preterm birth and perinatal mortality.

questions.text: ACE inhibitors (e.g., Ramipril) and ARBs (e.g., Losartan) reduce proteinuria and slow CKD progression primarily through which hemodynamically mediated renal mechanism?
options: Selective vasodilation of the efferent arteriole, reducing intraglomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure
Increasing systemic arterial blood pressure to augment GFR
questions.explanation: Angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole. Blocking its action vasodilates the efferent arteriole more than the afferent, reducing intraglomerular hyperfiltration, capillary wall tension, and protein trafficking across the glomerular basement membrane.

questions.text: SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., Dapagliflozin, Empagliflozin) confer powerful renoprotection in chronic kidney disease by restoring tubuloglomerular feedback through which mechanism?
options: Increasing sodium delivery to the macula densa, triggering afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction and reducing hyperfiltration
Dilating the efferent arteriole via bradykinin release
questions.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors block proximal sodium-glucose cotransport, delivering more sodium and chloride downstream to the macula densa. This restores tubuloglomerular feedback, constricting the inappropriately dilated afferent arteriole and reducing intraglomerular hypertension.

questions.text: Which non-calcium, non-aluminum phosphate binder is preferred in CKD patients with hyperphosphatemia and vascular calcification?
questions.explanation: Sevelamer is an anion-exchange, non-absorbable polymer that binds intestinal phosphate without adding calcium load, preventing the progression of arterial and valvular calcification in CKD.

questions.text: Cinacalcet is an allosteric activator of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) used in CKD stage 5 on dialysis to manage:
questions.explanation: Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic that increases the sensitivity of CaSR on the parathyroid glands to extracellular calcium, suppressing PTH secretion without increasing serum calcium or phosphate.

questions.text: When administering erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs, e.g., Epoetin alfa) in CKD patients with anemia, the target hemoglobin concentration should strictly NOT exceed:
questions.explanation: Target hemoglobin in CKD is maintained between 10.0 and 11.5 g/dL. Clinical trials demonstrated that normalizing hemoglobin above 12-13 g/dL with ESAs significantly increases the risk of stroke, myocardial infarction, and vascular access thrombosis.

questions.text: Oral sodium bicarbonate therapy is prescribed in chronic kidney disease stages 3 to 5 when serum bicarbonate falls below 22 mEq/L primarily to:
options: Alkalinize the stomach to enhance phosphate absorption
Slow the rate of GFR decline and reduce muscle protein catabolism
questions.explanation: Chronic metabolic acidosis in CKD stimulates endothelin and aldosterone, accelerates renal fibrogenesis, and triggers ubiquitin-proteasome muscle wasting. Sodium bicarbonate supplementation slows CKD progression and preserves muscle mass.

questions.text: Why are nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs, e.g., Ibuprofen, Diclofenac) strictly avoided in patients with established CKD?
options: They block vasodilatory renal prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2), causing acute afferent arteriolar constriction and precipitating acute-on-chronic renal failure
They cause severe proximal tubular glucosuria
They stimulate excessive renin and aldosterone release
questions.explanation: In CKD, renal perfusion depends critically on compensatory vasodilatory prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) maintaining afferent arteriolar patency. NSAID inhibition of COX blocks these prostaglandins, causing unopposed afferent constriction, acute GFR collapse, and hyperkalemia.

questions.text: Which potassium-binding polymer exchanges sodium for potassium in the gastrointestinal tract and is used for chronic outpatient management of hyperkalemia in CKD patients taking ACE inhibitors or ARBs?
questions.explanation: Novel potassium binders (Patiromer, SZC) bind potassium in the colon, allowing patients with advanced CKD and heart failure to safely maintain life-prolonging ACE inhibitor, ARB, or MRA therapy without developing recurrent hyperkalemia.

sources: Pharmacology/essay questions and MCQs urogenital part 3 and 4.pdf-p4-Q11
questions.text: Regarding Tadalafil in the management of erectile dysfunction and BPH, which pharmacological characteristic is correct?
options: It has a short half-life of 4 hours requiring dosing immediately before coitus
It selectively inhibits PDE-6 in retinal photoreceptors causing blue-tinted vision
It possesses an elimination half-life of ~17.5 hours, permitting once-daily dosing for both ED and BPH lower urinary tract symptoms
It directly stimulates testosterone production by Leydig cells
questions.explanation: Tadalafil has a prolonged elimination half-life (~17.5 hours) compared to sildenafil (4 hours). This unique pharmacokinetic property enables once-daily low-dose administration (5 mg) that improves both erectile function and BPH urinary symptoms.

sources: Pharmacology/essay questions and MCQs urogenital part 3 and 4.pdf-p4-Q12
questions.text: Phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE-5) inhibitors (e.g., Sildenafil, Tadalafil) are approved and clinically utilized for all the following indications EXCEPT:
options: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH lower urinary tract symptoms)
questions.explanation: PDE-5 inhibitors relax vascular smooth muscle (ED and pulmonary hypertension) and bladder neck/prostatic smooth muscle (BPH). They have no anti-neoplastic activity and are never indicated for treating prostate cancer.

sources: Pharmacology/essay questions and MCQs urogenital part 3 and 4.pdf-p5-Q19
questions.text: Finasteride improves lower urinary tract symptoms in BPH by which mechanism and over what typical timeframe?
options: Relaxing bladder neck alpha-1A receptors within 48 hours
Inhibiting 5alpha-reductase, reducing intraprostatic DHT and shrinking prostate volume over 3 to 6 months
Blocking Leydig cell LH receptors to eliminate testosterone
questions.explanation: Finasteride is an oral 5alpha-reductase inhibitor that blocks conversion of testosterone to DHT. By eliminating the trophic stimulation of DHT, it reduces prostate volume by ~20-25%, but requires 3 to 6 months of continuous therapy for maximal clinical benefit.

sources: Pharmacology/essay questions and MCQs urogenital part 3 and 4.pdf-p4-Q13
questions.text: Concurrent administration of PDE-5 inhibitors (e.g., Sildenafil) with organic nitrates (e.g., Nitroglycerin, Isosorbide mononitrate) is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED because:
options: It causes severe acute renal tubular necrosis
Synergistic elevation of cGMP in vascular smooth muscle produces profound, refractory hypotension and cardiovascular collapse
It precipitates acute priapism lasting >24 hours
Nitrates completely block the intestinal absorption of sildenafil
questions.explanation: Organic nitrates stimulate guanylyl cyclase to form cGMP, while PDE-5 inhibitors block cGMP breakdown. The massive accumulation of intracellular cGMP in vascular smooth muscle triggers profound systemic vasodilation, catastrophic hypotension, myocardial infarction, and death.

sources: Pharmacology/essay questions and MCQs urogenital part 3 and 4.pdf-p5-Q18
questions.text: Which adverse effect is characteristically associated with 5alpha-reductase inhibitor therapy (Finasteride/Dutasteride)?
options: Erectile dysfunction, decreased libido, and gynecomastia
questions.explanation: Suppressing DHT impairs androgenic signaling in target tissues, causing decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, ejaculatory disorders, and gynecomastia (due to increased peripheral aromatization of accumulating testosterone into estrogen).

sources: Pharmacology/essay questions and MCQs urogenital part 3 and 4.pdf-p4-Q15
questions.text: Which alpha-1 adrenergic antagonist exhibits high selectivity for the alpha-1A receptor subtype in the bladder neck and prostate, minimizing orthostatic hypotension?
questions.explanation: Tamsulosin and Silodosin are uroselective alpha-1A antagonists. They preferentially relax smooth muscle in the prostate stroma and bladder neck while having minimal effect on vascular alpha-1B receptors, thus minimizing systemic vasodilation and orthostatic hypotension.

questions.text: When initiating GnRH agonists (e.g., Leuprolide, Goserelin) for metastatic prostate cancer, a non-steroidal antiandrogen (e.g., Bicalutamide) must be co-administered during the first 2-4 weeks to prevent:
options: The initial testosterone 'flare' that can exacerbate bone pain, spinal cord compression, and urinary obstruction
questions.explanation: GnRH agonists initially stimulate pituitary GnRH receptors, triggering a surge of LH and FSH that causes a temporary 'flare' in serum testosterone during the first 1-2 weeks. Antiandrogens block androgen receptors during this window to prevent clinical flare.

questions.text: Which drug suppresses androgen synthesis in castration-resistant prostate cancer by irreversibly inhibiting the enzyme CYP17 (17alpha-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase)?
questions.explanation: Abiraterone acetate selectively and irreversibly inhibits CYP17A1 in the testes, adrenals, and prostate tumor tissue itself, completely shutting down de novo androgen biosynthesis (must be given with prednisone to prevent compensatory ACTH-driven mineralocorticoid excess).

sources: Pharmacology/essay questions and MCQs urogenital part 3 and 4.pdf-p6-Q21
questions.text: What is the definitive first-line pharmacological treatment of choice for primary and secondary syphilis?
options: Oral Doxycycline 100 mg BID for 14 days
Intramuscular Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units in a single dose
questions.explanation: Intramuscular Benzathine penicillin G (2.4 million units single dose) provides sustained treponemicidal blood levels for 3 to 4 weeks and remains the undisputed gold standard for primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis.

questions.text: An acute, self-limiting febrile reaction with chills, headache, and myalgias occurring within 24 hours of initiating penicillin therapy for syphilis is known as:
questions.explanation: The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is an acute inflammatory cascade caused by the massive lysis of spirochetes releasing endotoxin-like lipoproteins. It requires reassurance, antipyretics, and supportive care; penicillin therapy must NOT be stopped.

sources: Pharmacology/essay questions and MCQs urogenital part 3 and 4.pdf-p6-Q24
questions.text: In a pregnant patient treated with intramuscular Ceftriaxone for uncomplicated gonorrhea, which antibiotic is recommended if concurrent Chlamydia trachomatis infection is suspected?
options: Oral Doxycycline 100 mg BID for 7 days
Oral Azithromycin 1 gram in a single dose
questions.explanation: Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy due to fetal bone growth restriction and permanent deciduous tooth discoloration. Azithromycin (1g single oral dose) is Category B, safe in pregnancy, and effectively cures chlamydial infection.

sources: Pharmacology/essay questions and MCQs urogenital part 3 and 4.pdf-p6-Q25
questions.text: What is the antimicrobial drug of choice for trichomoniasis in both women and their sexual partners?
questions.explanation: Metronidazole (500 mg BID for 7 days, or 2g single dose) is the drug of choice for Trichomonas vaginalis. Because trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted ping-pong infection, simultaneous treatment of all sexual partners is mandatory.

questions.text: Patients taking Metronidazole must be strictly instructed to avoid consuming alcoholic beverages to prevent:
options: Severe disulfiram-like reaction (facial flushing, throbbing headache, nausea, tachycardia, hypotension)
questions.explanation: Metronidazole inhibits hepatic aldehyde dehydrogenase. Ingestion of alcohol leads to accumulation of acetaldehyde, triggering an unpleasant and potentially dangerous disulfiram-like reaction with flushing, vomiting, and palpitations.

sources: Pharmacology/essay questions and MCQs urogenital part 3 and 4.pdf-p6-Q26
questions.text: What is the primary antiviral mechanism of action of Acyclovir and Valacyclovir in suppressing genital herpes simplex virus (HSV-2) outbreaks?
options: Selective phosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase, leading to inhibition of viral DNA polymerase and chain termination
Inhibition of viral neuraminidase preventing viral egress
Inhibition of viral protease cleavage of capsid polyproteins
Blockade of viral uncoating in host endosomes
questions.explanation: Acyclovir is selectively monophosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase, then converted by host cellular kinases to acyclovir triphosphate, which competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase and acts as an obligate DNA chain terminator.

sources: Pharmacology/essay questions and MCQs urogenital part 3 and 4.pdf-p6-Q27
questions.text: What is the current first-line empirical regimen recommended by CDC and international guidelines for uncomplicated anogenital gonorrhea?
options: Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly in a single dose
questions.explanation: Due to widespread fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and penicillin resistance, Ceftriaxone (500 mg IM single dose for patients <150 kg) is the recommended first-line monotherapy for uncomplicated gonorrhea.

questions.text: Which patient-applied topical medication is approved for external genital warts (condyloma acuminata) that acts as an immune response modifier by stimulating toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7) and inducing interferon-alpha?
questions.explanation: Imiquimod is a synthetic TLR7 agonist that stimulates local dendritic cells to release interferon-alpha, interleukin-12, and TNF-alpha, activating a cell-mediated immune response that clears HPV-induced genital warts.

questions.text: What is the primary mechanism of action by which combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptives (COCs) prevent pregnancy?
options: Direct toxic effect on spermatozoa in the vagina
Suppression of hypothalamic-pituitary gonadotropin secretion (LH and FSH), thereby preventing ovulation
Accelerated transport of the ovum through the fallopian tube
questions.explanation: Estrogen suppresses pituitary FSH release (preventing follicle selection), while the progestin suppresses the midcycle LH surge, thereby completely blocking ovulation. Progestins also thicken cervical mucus and atrophy the endometrium.

questions.text: How does Raloxifene differ fundamentally from Tamoxifen in its organ-specific estrogenic effects?

Raloxifene causes bone loss and severe osteoporosis
Raloxifene is completely devoid of venous thromboembolism risk
questions.explanation: Raloxifene is an estrogen agonist on bone (preserving bone mineral density in postmenopausal osteoporosis) and lipid metabolism, but acts as an antagonist on BOTH breast and endometrial tissues, meaning it does NOT increase endometrial cancer risk.

sources: Pharmacology/essay questions and MCQs urogenital part 3 and 4.pdf-p2-Q3
questions.text: Clomiphene citrate induces ovulation in anovulatory infertility (such as polycystic ovary syndrome) by which mechanism?
options: Antagonizing estrogen receptors in the hypothalamus, blocking negative feedback and increasing pulsatile GnRH and gonadotropin (FSH/LH) release
Aromatizing androgens directly into estrogens within the follicle
Acting as an agonist on progesterone receptors
questions.explanation: Clomiphene binds hypothalamic estrogen receptors and prevents normal estradiol negative feedback. The hypothalamus perceives a hypoestrogenic state, releasing more pulsatile GnRH, which drives pituitary FSH and LH secretion to trigger follicular growth and ovulation.

questions.explanation: Women aged >= 35 who smoke have an exponentially increased risk of serious cardiovascular events, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and stroke due to estrogen-induced hepatic procoagulant synthesis (Fibrinogen, Factors VII, VIII, X) combined with nicotine-induced endothelial damage.

questions.explanation: Ethinyl estradiol stimulates hepatic synthesis of clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X, fibrinogen) and decreases antithrombin III, conferring a 2- to 4-fold elevated risk of venous thromboembolism. Progestins contribute to acne, weight gain, and mood changes.

questions.explanation: Estrogens suppress prolactin-mediated lactation and reduce breast milk volume and composition. Progestin-only pills (POPs) do not affect lactation or milk quantity and carry no thromboembolic risk, making them the oral method of choice postpartum.

questions.text: Mention the pathogenic role of the following virulence factors in their associated clinical infections: 1) Protein A of Staphylococcus aureus; 2) Urease of Proteus mirabilis; 3) Listeriolysin O of Listeria monocytogenes:
questions.explanation: Authoritative Ain Shams virulence factor pathogenesis.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Protein A (Staphylococcus aureus): Cell wall surface protein that binds to the Fc fragment of IgG antibodies in reverse orientation, preventing antibody-mediated opsonization and phagocytosis by neutrophils.
2. Urease (Proteus mirabilis): Cleaves urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, alkalinizing the urine (pH > 7.2). This precipitates magnesium ammonium phosphate to form staghorn (struvite) calculi, promoting persistent UTI, urothelial injury, and renal parenchymal obstruction.
3. Listeriolysin O (Listeria monocytogenes): A pore-forming cholesterol-dependent cytolysin that disrupts the phagosomal membrane, allowing internalized bacteria to escape into host cell cytoplasm to replicate and spread cell-to-cell.

questions.text: Mention one bacterial cause and primary mode/source of infection for each of the following clinical presentations: 1) Undulant fever; 2) Rice-water diarrhea; 3) Subacute bacterial endocarditis on pre-existing damaged valves:
questions.explanation: Authoritative Ain Shams bacterial etiology and epidemiology.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Undulant Fever: Causative organism: Brucella melitensis (or B. abortus / B. suis). Mode/source: Ingestion of unpasteurized dairy products (raw milk, soft cheese) or direct occupational contact with infected livestock tissues.
2. Rice-Water Diarrhea: Causative organism: Vibrio cholerae (serogroups O1 or O139). Mode/source: Fecal-oral route through ingestion of water or seafood contaminated with human fecal material.
3. Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis: Causative organism: Streptococcus viridans (e.g., S. sanguinis, S. mitis). Mode/source: Transient bacteremia following dental manipulation or vigorous mastication in patients with pre-existing valvular disease.

questions.text: Discuss the following immunological topics: 1) Two immune mechanisms mediating acute allograft rejection; 2) Three clinical therapeutic applications of monoclonal antibodies; 3) Key cytokines produced by regulatory T (Treg) cells:
questions.explanation: Authoritative Ain Shams immunological mechanisms and therapeutics.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Acute Allograft Rejection Mechanisms:
   - Cellular Rejection: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells recognize foreign donor HLA class I and destroy graft parenchymal cells via perforin/granzyme; CD4+ Th1 cells secrete IFN-γ, recruiting alloreactive macrophages.
   - Humoral (Antibody-Mediated) Rejection: Recipient antibodies against donor HLA molecules activate the classical complement pathway, causing acute necrotizing vasculitis and graft thrombosis.
2. Three Applications of Monoclonal Antibodies:
   - Oncological: Trastuzumab (anti-HER2 in breast cancer), Rituximab (anti-CD20 in lymphoma).
   - Autoimmune/Anti-inflammatory: Infliximab / Adalimumab (anti-TNF-α in rheumatoid arthritis and IBD).
   - Organ Transplantation: Basiliximab (anti-IL-2Rα / CD25 to prevent acute allograft rejection).
3. Cytokines Produced by Regulatory T (Treg) Cells:
   - Transforming Growth Factor-beta (TGF-β) and Interleukin-10 (IL-10), both of which suppress effector T cell proliferation and inhibit pro-inflammatory cytokine production.

questions.text: Discuss the following immunological topics: 1) Two immune mechanisms mediating acute allograft rejection; 2) Three clinical therapeutic applications of monoclonal antibodies; 3) Key cytokines produced by regulatory T (Treg) cells:
questions.explanation: Authoritative Ain Shams immunology review.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Acute Allograft Rejection Mechanisms:
   - Cellular Rejection: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells recognize donor HLA class I antigens and mediate target cell lysis; CD4+ Th1 cells secrete cytokines that activate macrophages.
   - Humoral Rejection: Pre-existing or de novo donor-specific antibodies bind to graft endothelial cells and trigger complement-mediated vascular destruction.
2. Three Applications of Monoclonal Antibodies:
   - Cancer therapy: Trastuzumab (HER2+ breast cancer), Rituximab (CD20+ B-cell lymphoma).
   - Autoimmune diseases: Infliximab (anti-TNF-α for rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn's disease).
